name: Nosemaxxing

lead: Nosemaxxing is an umbrella term for anything done to make the nose look better balanced with the rest of the face. It spans surgical rhinoplasty, non-surgical filler work, and softer measures that forum members describe, such as losing weight, trying nasal exercises or treating a puffy-looking nose.

The appearance payoff people describe is a straighter profile, a slimmer or less swollen look, or a tip and bridge that sit better with the eyes and chin. Surgery has a long clinical literature; the home methods are discussed mainly in community threads.

paras: Members of looksmax.org discuss a ladder of options. At the low-effort end are weight loss (some say facial fat makes the nose look bigger), skincare aimed at a bloated or oily nose, and daily nasal muscle exercises. Further up are filler-based non-surgical rhinoplasty and surgical rhinoplasty performed by a surgeon. Some members treat the first group as a way to refine the nose, others call it a stopgap until surgery.

Rhinoplasty carries the usual surgical risks, swelling that can take a year or more to settle, and a revision rate the medical literature puts at roughly 5 to 20 percent. Fillers and prescription skincare have their own side-effect profiles that a clinician explains. No published trials have tested whether nasal exercises change nose shape.

angle.text: People pursue nosemaxxing to change nose shape or to reduce a swollen, bulky look. Surgery and fillers change structure directly; weight loss, skincare and exercises are described by members as ways of softening the nose's appearance.

lead: Nosemaxxing is a term from looksmaxxing communities for improving the appearance of the nose. The nose sits at the center of the face, and forum members often name it as the feature they most want to change; one poster on looksmax.org described a long nose as his biggest flaw [1].

Methods discussed under the label range from medical to home-based. Surgical rhinoplasty is the established route for reshaping the nose and is divided by clinicians into open and closed approaches and into cosmetic and functional operations [2]. Injectable fillers, known as non-surgical or liquid rhinoplasty, can make a nose look straighter by adding volume to selected spots, though they cannot reduce its size [3]. Community threads also cover weight loss, nasal exercises, and measures for a nose that looks swollen or oily [1][4][5].

Researchers have studied rhinoplasty and filler rhinoplasty extensively, including patient satisfaction, complications and the rate of body dysmorphic disorder among candidates [6][6]. The softer methods, such as exercising nasal muscles to change cartilage shape, appear mainly in forum posts, and no published trials were located that test them.

paras: Nosemaxxing groups together every method used to make the nose look better. Community threads usually split it into a surgical tier (rhinoplasty), a minimally invasive tier (fillers) and a no-surgery tier of lifestyle and self-care measures [4][7]. The tiers are sometimes described as a ladder: members who try the cheapest rung first may later move to a clinic, and others treat each rung as a separate goal.

Aesthetic planning in rhinoplasty refers to measures such as the nasofrontal and nasolabial angles, which describe the profile where the nose meets the forehead and the upper lip [2]. These terms occasionally appear in looksmaxxing discussion of profile harmony, where the nose is judged alongside the eyes, chin and jaw.

One long-running looksmax.org thread credits weight loss with a changed nose, arguing that body fat makes the nose look larger, and recommends getting leaner first [4]. The poster presents it as the first step before anything else; the claim is anecdotal and rests on before-and-after photos in the thread.

The same thread describes doing nose exercises from videos each day on the theory that cartilage could be reshaped over time [4]. Another thread shares a hospital handout of nasal muscle exercises and asks whether this approach is worthwhile or merely cope; one reply says that anything not involving real risk is cope [5]. A further thread titled around nosemaxxing without surgery or makeup collects non-surgical suggestions [7]. A search of the biomedical literature turned up no study that tests exercises for changing nose shape.

A teenager on looksmax.org asked about a nose that retains water and looks puffy despite having no acne, noting that others use isotretinoin or hydrocortisone for the same look and asking about side effects [1]. Such posts are individual questions, not clinical guidance.

Non-surgical rhinoplasty uses injectable fillers to reshape the nose. It is augmentation only, so it adds volume rather than removing it, but it can make a nose look smaller by making it look straighter; common targets are a low bridge, tip projection and bumps [3]. Hyaluronic acid fillers are temporary and can be dissolved with the enzyme hyaluronidase, while calcium hydroxyapatite fillers last longer and cannot be reversed [3]. Permanent options such as liquid silicone, polyacrylamide gel and PMMA exist; some studies report more complications with polyacrylamide gel, which is not FDA-approved [3].

A 2024 systematic review in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery covered 23 articles with 3,928 patients treated with hyaluronic acid. The nasal tip was the most frequently injected site, nasal hump deformities were the most common reason for treatment, all studies reported high patient satisfaction, and eight patients developed major complications [6]. A 2021 review of eight studies with 674 patients found 98.2 percent satisfied or very satisfied in the weeks after injection and 96.4 percent at one year, with effects lasting 8 to 14 months [6]. A critical review of complications found little high-level evidence and suggested complications may be under-reported; it emphasised early recognition and having hyaluronidase available for serious events such as vascular occlusion [6].

Clinical sources describe rhinoplasty as open or closed, primary or revision, and cosmetic or functional. Open rhinoplasty adds a small incision across the columella and gives the surgeon better visualisation of the tip; closed rhinoplasty uses only incisions inside the nose and is associated with less swelling and faster recovery. Systematic reviews cited by Wikipedia found no significant long-term difference in patient-reported scores between the two [2]. Revision surgery is needed in roughly 5 to 20 percent of cases, and swelling can take at least a year to resolve [2].

A 2020 systematic review of 29 articles on patient satisfaction found that most studies reported higher satisfaction after surgery, whether using conventional structural techniques or newer preservation techniques, with the authors noting that preservation rhinoplasty needs more study [6].

Nose reconstruction long predates cosmetic surgery. Wikipedia traces it to Egyptian papyri, to the Sushruta Samhita, which describes rebuilding a nose with a cheek flap, and to Celsus in Rome [2]. Gasparo Tagliacozzi described an arm-flap method in 1597, and Joseph Constantine Carpue and Karl Ferdinand von Graefe published operations in the early nineteenth century [2].

The modern cosmetic operation is usually dated to the late nineteenth century. John Orlando Roe performed the first modern closed (endonasal) rhinoplasty in 1887, and Jacques Joseph described nose reduction through internal incisions in 1928 [2]. Open rhinoplasty was introduced by Aurel Rethi in 1934 and later promoted by surgeons such as Padovan, Goodman and Jack Gunter [2]. Ultrasonic bone shaping was introduced in 2004 [2].

Body dysmorphic disorder is a recurring theme in the surgical literature on the nose. A 2016 systematic review estimated weighted prevalence at 20.1 percent in rhinoplasty patients, compared with 1.9 percent in community adults [6]. A 2023 meta-analysis of 18 studies and 2,132 candidates reported a pooled prevalence of 32.7 percent with wide variation between studies and screening tools [6]. Surgeons commonly screen candidates for such concerns before operating.

Researchers have also written about the role of social media in nasal aesthetics. A 2026 narrative review linked exposure to before-and-after photos, influencer endorsements and filtered images with greater interest in rhinoplasty and raised concerns about unrealistic expectations [6]. Wikipedia notes that a #NoseJobCheck trend on TikTok from late 2020 to early 2021 reached over a billion views [2].

Rhinoplasty risks include prolonged swelling, asymmetry and the need for revision [2]. Wikipedia notes that smoking can compromise healing [2]. For fillers, infection, haematoma, asymmetry and granulomas are listed, and filler entering a blood vessel can block circulation and cause skin necrosis; hyaluronic acid fillers can be reversed with hyaluronidase [3][6]. Isotretinoin and topical corticosteroids mentioned in forum threads are prescription medicines with their own labelled side effects; no studies were located on using them for nose puffiness in people without acne [1].

No studies found on nosemaxxing as a practice or on nasal exercises for changing nose shape. Rhinoplasty and filler rhinoplasty are the subject of a broad surgical literature summarised above [6][6][6].

Forum users disagree about what counts as meaningful. Some call non-surgical nosemaxxing cope and say only surgery changes the nose; others share routines they credit for improvement [4][5]. One member said they had always thought nosemaxxing was cope but wanted to try it [4]. The term sits among other single-feature labels such as eyemaxxing and jawmaxxing, and threads on it are comparatively sparse next to those topics, a point one reply makes by saying the forum has a severe lack of nosemaxxing threads [4].

lore.intro: Nosemaxxing threads on looksmax.org mix personal before-and-after posts, questions from younger members, and debate over whether non-surgical methods are worthwhile [1][4][5].
